Does the model already understand the problem it is failing?

Highlights from experiments 0, 1 and 3 · Qwen/Qwen3-4B, seed 0 · 52 implication laws × 6 surface forms = 312 texts · formalizations graded by the deterministic checkform parser.

Summary

By the middle of the stack the model holds a representation of which law a problem is that survives a complete change of wording — we read it out at 86% against a 1.9% chance rate.

Pushing the model along the story → literal-NL direction with a steering vector changes task accuracy by exactly nothing. What separates 10% accuracy from 90% is the number of thinking tokens the model is allowed to write, and narrative framing costs roughly a 2× budget multiplier over its literal-NL twin.

So the bottleneck looks like serial compute, not representation style. "Represent this as a math problem rather than a story" is not the missing step, because the model has largely done that already and still fails.

1. What the raw text already gives away (exp 0)

Fix the floor first

Every problem in the set is one implication between algebraic laws, rendered six ways: four themed stories with near-disjoint vocabulary (graft, paint, signal, tea), one literal natural-language description, and one Rigid Grammar rendering such as ASSUME: va = op(va, va).

Surface form is the geometry of text space — but the forms are not a ladder

Below is a PCA of the 312 texts as word-TF-IDF vectors: no model, no activations, just which words each text uses.

The axes turn out to be form indicators. PC1 correlates with "is this Rigid Grammar" at r = +0.995 and PC2 with "is this literal-NL" at r = +0.972 — recovered with no labels at all, because that is genuinely where the variance is. PC1 also correlates with word count at r = −0.881, so even this dominant axis conflates being formal with being short.

Form separation is free. Mean cosine similarity within a surface group is 0.91–0.99 against 0.00–0.17 between groups, and Rigid Grammar shares exactly zero vocabulary with the stories.

But the three forms are not an ordered progression. If formality were a single axis, the literal-NL centroid would sit about halfway along the story → RG line.

Does this depend on the featurization?

No. The same picture holds for character n-grams and for LSA-100, a dense 100-dimensional embedding.

2. Evidence for semantic core (exp 3)

Run the same retrieval on the residual stream and the picture inverts. Law identity rises steeply through the first half of the network, peaks at 86% around layers 18–24, then falls back as the model re-specialises for next-token prediction.

Activation-based PCA

In a plain 2D projection of the activations, 72–100% of the variance is surface form — essentially one axis separating Rigid Grammar from natural language. The four story themes pile on top of each other and literal NL sits apart from both, with no clean story → literal → RG ladder. This is the same arrangement section 1 found in the raw text, which is exactly why it is context rather than a result: form separation was already free. Reading law identity out takes the nearest-neighbour analysis above, not the top components. One interesting observation here is in the 2 right-most plots, the Signal-stories seem to deviate away from the story cluster a bit more, towards literal-NL cluster.

Colour by complexity

Colouring the same projections by operation count gives an ordered gradient rather than clusters, clearest along the Rigid Grammar arm. But exp 0 found that word count correlates with operation count at r = 0.93–1.00 within every surface form, so this is a length gradient until it is shown to survive residualization — a check that has not been run. It is a property of the dataset, not of the plot; the clean fix is length-matched instances upstream.

3. Steering along story → literal does nothing (exp 1)

Clean null

If narrative framing is what breaks the model, then moving activations along the story → literal-NL difference direction should help. It does not. The vector itself is real — per-pair differences cohere at cosine 0.63–0.91, so it is a consistent direction rather than an average of noise — but across a layer × dose sweep, α = 1 is indistinguishable from doing nothing.

Two details make the null informative rather than merely disappointing:

  • α = 1 does register. Diffing cached generations against baseline, the text differs on 52/52 examples, so the logits move on every input. They just move nothing directional.
  • The ceiling for this intervention was always low. Literal-NL with no thinking scores 19.2% against story's 9.6%, so even a perfect story → literal conversion buys about 10 points, not the ~80 points of the thinking-mode gap.

The remaining unexplored variable is the injection site, not the dose: the current hook adds the vector at every token position during prefill and decode, much heavier than the literature usually applies.

4. What actually moves accuracy: thinking budget (exp 1 and exp 3)

Main driver

Cap thinking tokens at B, splice in </think> when the budget runs out, and grade what comes next. Both wordings are flat and near the floor until B = 256, then climb steeply.

budget Bstoryliteral-NLstory, exp 3's own sweep

641.9%19.2%11.5%
1281.9%17.3%17.3%
25611.5%36.5%25.0%
51238.5%96.2%44.2%
102478.8%100%—
∞90.4%——

Three things to take from this:

  • Small budgets are actively harmful. Story accuracy at B = 32–128 sits below the B = 0 floor: a cut-off trace leaves a half-finished draft and the grader scores the draft. Worth confirming this is a grading artifact rather than a real effect.
  • Narrative framing costs about a 2× budget multiplier. Literal-NL hits 96% at B = 512 where story needs B = 1024 to reach 79%. That is a fairly direct measurement of the token cost of de-narrativizing.
  • The story arm has not saturated at B = 1024 — only 4/52 traces closed naturally — so 79% is still climbing toward the 90.4% unlimited ceiling. Breaking exp 3's sweep down by problem size shows where the budget goes: at B = 512, 100% correct on 1–2 operations, 55% on 3–4, 40% on 5–8.
